pl-l3d15c2-d1e117.summary: Explains, so that no contradiction is thought to exist in sacred writings, that these authorities remove from Christ not the truth of fear and sorrow, nor propassio, but the necessity of fear and sorrow, and passio.
claims: The authorities deny necessity and passio in Christ, not true fear and sorrow.

pl-l3d15c2-d1e120.summary: Develops the distinction: Christ had true fear and sorrow in his human nature, but not as we, his members, do. We are subject to these defects necessarily because of sin, and in us they are both propassio and passio, in Christ only propassio. As in sins, so in penal affections there are grades: when one is affected by fear or sorrow without the mind being moved from rectitude or contemplation of God, it is propassio; when it is moved and disturbed, passio. Christ was never so disturbed as to decline from rectitude or contemplation of God; in this sense he is said not to have feared or been sad.
claims: In Christ fear and sorrow were only propassio.
Propassio leaves the mind's rectitude undisturbed; passio disturbs it.

pl-l3d15c2-d1e123.summary: Cites Jerome on Mt 26:37 ('he began to be sorrowful'): to prove the truth of the assumed man, he was truly saddened, but passio did not dominate his mind; it was propassio, hence 'began to be sorrowful'. To be sad differs from beginning to be sad, as propassio from passio. By this distinction Christ is sometimes said not truly to have feared, sometimes truly to have feared: he had true fear and sorrow, but not as passio or by necessity of condition.
claims: Christ had true fear and sorrow, but not as passio.

pl-l3d15c2-d1e142.summary: Cites Augustine, wishing his words understood according to these causes, saying Christ did not truly fear or grieve and immediately that he had true sorrow: prefiguring the weak in himself, the Lord said 'let this cup pass'; he did not truly fear to suffer, to rise on the third day, when Paul longed to be dissolved. This seems to remove sorrow and fear from Christ.
claims: Augustine seems to deny fear and sorrow in Christ.

pl-l3d15c2-d1e154.summary: Continues Augustine: but he took sorrow as he took flesh. He was sad, as the Gospel says; if not, then when it says he slept, he did not sleep, or ate, he did not eat, and nothing sound would remain, and one would say even his body was not true. Whatever is written of him is true and happened; so he was sad, taking true sorrow by will as he took true flesh by will.
claims: Christ took true sorrow by will as he took true flesh.
Denying Christ's sorrow would undermine all the Gospel says of him.

pl-l3d15c2-d1e163.summary: Observes that Augustine would contradict himself in these words unless he distinguished the different causes from which the sense of his statements must be taken; once the reason for each is discerned, there is no contradiction.
claims: Augustine's statements are consistent when their senses are distinguished.

pl-l3d15c2.summary: Reconciles the authorities: they deny in Christ not the truth of fear and sorrow, nor propassio, but the necessity of fear and sorrow and passio. Christ had true fear and sorrow, but not as we do: in us they are necessary, due to sin, and occur both as propassio and passio; in him only as propassio, affecting him without moving his mind from rectitude or contemplation of God. Jerome's 'he began to be sorrowful' marks propassio. Augustine both denies and affirms Christ's sorrow, which is no contradiction once the different senses are distinguished: Christ took true sorrow by will, as he took true flesh.
claims: Christ had true fear and sorrow, but as propassio, not passio.
Christ's fear and sorrow were not necessary but voluntary.
Christ's affections did not move his mind from rectitude or contemplation of God.
Apparent contradictions in the authorities dissolve when their senses are distinguished.
